De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Timer block diagram Prescaler → CK_scaled • The chip clock is usually too fast for the counter • The prescaler divides it by a chosen factor (e.g. ÷1000) • Output is a slower tick, CK_scaled → this sets how fast the counter counts Auto-Reload Register Capture&Compare Register counter prescaler CK_in CK_scaled External Input MUX Trigger Event MR Count Compare PWM Trigger Event PWM

De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Timer block diagram External input (via the MUX) A MUX selects what actually drives the counter: • CK_scaled → the counter measures time (internal clock) • External Input → the counter counts external pulses, not time • Same timer, two uses: timebase or event/pulse counter Auto-Reload Register Capture&Compare Register counter prescaler CK_in CK_scaled External Input MUX Trigger Event MR Count Compare PWM Trigger Event PWM

De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Timer block diagram Counter • Driven by the tick chosen in the MUX; each tick adds 1 → the current value is the Count • MR = the reset input: it brings the count back to 0 • Counter can be set in Up, Down, Up/Down mode. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Timer block diagram Trigger Event • When count = Auto- Reload value, Compare fires a Trigger Event • That event resets the counter (via MR) → it starts again from 0 • So the counter runs in a loop; the length of the loop = the period Auto-Reload Register Capture&Compare Register counter prescaler CK_in CK_scaled External Input MUX Trigger Event MR Count Compare PWM Trigger Event PWM

# Page 12^page=12
15 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Timer block diagram The PWM block compares the count to the Capture&Compare register: • Output is high while count is below the threshold, low above it • The counter ramps up and resets every period, so the output becomes a repeating square wave = PWM Auto-Reload Register Capture&Compare Register counter prescaler CK_in CK_scaled External Input MUX Trigger Event MR Count Compare PWM Trigger Event PWM Period / frequency ← prescaler + Auto-Reload Duty cycle ← Capture & Compare

# Page 13^page=13
17 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Timer structure Trigger / clock controller: • selects input clock • synchronization with other clocks (Master → Output Trigger Slave → Input Trigger) Prescaler Divides the frequency the counter increases, skipping a portion of the incoming events. Counter Up, Down, Up/Down counter Capture and Compare registers One for each channel Auto-reload register Sets the timer FSR

# Page 14^page=14
19 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Timer functionalities Time base Generates triggers and interrupts at the overflow (or at the ARR value) (e.g., trigger ADC conversion, software management, generic interrupts). Input capture Capture the counter value in the capture register. This allows the timer to record the time at which an externa event occurs. Output compare Every time that the compare value is reached: • corresponding output pin is SET/RESET/TOGGLE/UNCHANGED • generate an interrupt / trigger PWM generation • Edge aligned: counter Up or Down mode • Center aligned: counter Up/Down mode

# Page 15^page=15

# Page 17^page=17
22 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Registers Prescaler (PSC) Note that in order to divide by N the clock frequency you need to write N-1 in the Prescaler register Auto Reload Register (ARR) → named “period” in the CubeMX FSR of the counter (counter overflow) Capture / Compare Register (one for each channel) (CCRx) → named “pulse” in the CubeMX Capture = counter value when trigger is received Compare = counter value which generate an event (trigger or PWM commutation). A complete list of the timer registers can be found in the Reference Manual.

# Page 20^page=20
25 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Project 2a: Blinking LED (PWM) Objective of this project is to blink the NUCLEO board green LED at 1 Hz with 50% DC, using a PWM.

# Page 21^page=21
26 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Project 2a hints • Use the NUCLEO board Manual to find the GPIO connected to the green LED. • Set in CUBE the GPIO of the green LED as the output of a PWM • Check the TIMER clock frequency and configure the corresponding timer in order to obtain the required frequency and duty cycle. • Generate the c code. • In the main, start the correct channel of the timer connected to the LED. • Debug and verify the blinking frequency.

# Page 22^page=22
27 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Project 2b: Play note through speaker Objective of this project is to play a tone for 3 seconds using the speaker, using a PWM. Timer configuration for the various notes can be computed using the file “Musical notes.xslx” available on WeBeep

# Page 23^page=23
28 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Project 2b hints • Use the NUCLEO board Manual to find the GPIO connected to the speaker. • Set in CUBE the GPIO of the speaker as the output of a PWM • Check the TIMER clock frequency and configure the corresponding timer in order to obtain a 440 Hz tone (LA4 / A4 note) with 50 % duty cycle. • Generate the c code. • In the main, start the correct channel of the timer connected to the speaker. Stop it a few seconds later. • Debug and verify the note frequency. (Spectrum analyzer apps are easily available for smartphones)

# Page 24^page=24
29 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems HOMEWORK 3 Objective of this project is to play a song using the speaker when the microphone detects a loud sound. Try to use a timer interrupt to move through the notes and not the HAL_Delay function.

# Page 25^page=25
30 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems HOMEWORK 3 Timer configuration for the various notes can be computed using the file “Musical notes.xslx” available on WeBeep

# Page 26^page=26
31 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems HOMEWORK 3 Hint: start from playing a song once, without the microphone interrupt. • Start from the same configuration as in the previous project. • Identify the setup functions that initialize the timer frequency and pulse duration. • Use the required code from those functions to create a new function to setup a new frequency and pulse duration of the timer. • Define a struct to store the note frequency and duration • Create an array of structs to store the song • Play the song by stepping through the array, every time setting the correct frequency and for the correct duration of the note.

# Page 27^page=27
32 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems HOMEWORK 3 Now add the microphone interrupt! • Start from the same configuration as in the previous project. • Setup the correct interrupt and using the correct callback, play the song • Is the song being played correctly? If not, try to debug your code and propose a possible solution to the problem. • If the song is playing correctly, does it stop at the end? If not, debug your code and propose a possible solution to the problem.

# Page 28^page=28
33 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems HOMEWORK 3 Pin settings: • EXTI8 – PA8 (D7): microphone, rising edge, starts the song • TIM1 CH2 (PWM) – PA9 (D8): generates the note frequency for the buzzer • TIM2 (update interrupt): measures note duration

We need to multiply it by 10 to convert it in 1 ms. So, to obtain the value of the ARR for a specific note we need to do: 𝑁𝑜𝑡𝑒 𝑑𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑖𝑛 𝑡𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑜 ∗ 𝑇𝐸𝑀𝑃𝑂 ∗ 10 = 3 ∗ 75 𝑚𝑠 ∗ 10 𝑡𝑖𝑐𝑘𝑠 𝑚𝑠
